### `reports/calibration_toolbox_note_2026-10-03.md`

#### Calibration-toolbox metrics and the full rerun (3 Oct 2026)

Written before the rerun. These are **added descriptive metrics**; no decision rule or pre-set criterion changes.

##### What was added
- Toolbox: calibration-toolbox v0.1.0 (Pearce, MIT), `third_party/calibration-toolbox` @ 1c6f60bc; its 52 tests pass.
- Wrapper: `mondrian/calibration.py`.
  - A binary forecast p is passed as the two-class array [1−p, p].
  - Metrics: SCE, ECE (top-label), ACE (equal-mass bins), MCE, RMSCE and OE, all with the toolbox default of 15 bins.
  - For two classes, SCE equals the binary ECE of p against Y. `tests/test_calibration_metrics.py` checks this to within 1e-12.
  - **SCE is the headline calibration metric.** ECE/MCE/RMSCE/OE are reported in the appendix only.
- Where it is attached:
  - **Granularity** (`e5v2.forecast_arms`): per arm, averaged over procedures. It also gives NB-corrected SCE/ACE contrasts for G4−R, Gcv−R, MC−R, D−R and G4−D. These are secondary and outside the Holm family.
  - **Label-Free-Transfer** (`e8_transport.evaluate`), and therefore **Controlled-Shifts** and **PopQA-Elicit (E9c)** too.
  - **Failure-Modes**: every forecast arm under every shift.
  - **Real-Geometry**: SCE per arm.
  - **PopQA-Elicit (E9b)**, through `e5v2`.
- New figure: `experiments.fig_reliability` produces reliability diagrams for Label-Free-Transfer, pooling test predictions over 50 E8 splits.

##### Caveats stated in advance
- Binned ECE-type metrics are biased upward at small test sizes, and TruthfulQA test folds have about 272 questions. Compare arms at equal n; do not read the absolute values as calibration error.
- SCE measures forecast calibration, not set coverage. A map can calibrate well while losing resolution. Example: paired isotonic for Mistral compresses forecasts into [0.38, 0.55].

##### First look (fig_reliability, before the rerun)
Pooled SCE for the same procedure, no map, the quantile map and paired isotonic:

| Case | Same procedure | No map | Quantile map | Paired isotonic |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mistral, reversed | 0.016 | 0.335 | 0.053 | 0.032 |
| Mistral, reworded | 0.016 | 0.325 | 0.070 | 0.031 |
| Trained q reporter, reversed | 0.014 | 0.722 | 0.260 | 0.016 |

- The q-reporter row agrees with Prop. transport (b): that change is decreasing, so the quantile map, which is monotone increasing, cannot undo it, and paired isotonic does.
- Paired isotonic gets the lower SCE in every case, even where the quantile map gives better coverage. This is the coverage-versus-calibration distinction above.

##### Full rerun
- `python -m experiments.run_all --jobs 3` reruns every experiment and figure under one source hash. `--popqa` adds PopQA-Elicit and Failure-Modes PopQA once the reports are downloaded.
- The manifest is `runs/run_all_manifest.json`, and `--check` verifies it.
- Bug found while wiring this: `python -m experiments.fig_e5` never regenerated `fig_main`, because the `__main__` block came before that function's definition. Fixed; fig_main is now rebuilt by the runner.

### `reports/transport_controls_note_2026-10-03.md`

#### Transport controls and map variants (dated note, 3 Oct 2026, written before running)

**Motivation:** an external design review. Its points are checked against the code in the session log of 3 Oct. The author approved the work ("yes pleaae").

**Unchanged:**
- Every existing arm, so all reported numbers stay comparable.
- All criteria in the E8, E9 and E10 notes.

The additions are descriptive controls and variants. No new pass/fail criterion is introduced.

##### Setting (as implemented)
- y is the correctness of one stated candidate. It is teacher-forced and chosen by a label-blind hash.
- Sets are subsets of {0,1}.
- The nonconformity score is s(x,y) = 1 − p̂(y), where p̂ is a forecaster of the elicited report.
- Cells come from the frozen representation (E8/E9c: M = 4 farthest-first; Tinker: one cell), so transport is a score-within-fixed-cells experiment.
- Threshold k = ⌈(n+1)(1−α)⌉. The threshold is infinite when k > n or n < 20. There is no pooled fallback.

##### Additions

1. **Mid-rank quantile map (`ot_quantile_mid`).**
   - Stored from the transport fold only, then frozen: the sorted fit sample of V_B and V_A.
   - F_B^mid(v) = (#{V_B < v} + ½·#{V_B = v}) / n, clipped to [½/n, 1 − ½/n].
   - The reference quantile uses the inverse-CDF convention (`numpy.quantile`, `method="inverted_cdf"`).
   - Nothing depends on the evaluation batch.
   - Limitation: with atoms (ties) no deterministic map can match the marginals exactly. The tie fraction of each report is reported.
2. **Forced-direction isotonic (`paired_iso_inc`, `paired_iso_dec`).** Both directions are reported, alongside the existing fit-chosen arm. The direction is fixed by the arm name, before calibration.
3. **Known-inverse oracle (E10 only, `oracle_inverse`).** It applies the true noiseless inverse g⁻¹(v) = σ((logit v − b)/s) of the synthetic change. At σ = 0 it must reproduce A's sets exactly; for σ > 0 it separates the true map from estimation error.
   - The identity control is the existing "none" shift in E12 and the `naive` arm (an identity map) under no shift.
   - The rank-permutation control is the existing E12 `reorder_ρ` shifts.
4. **Signed per-cell gap.** For each arm: the per-cell coverage minus (1−α) over the frozen cells, given as min and max (`cell_gap_min`, `cell_gap_max`), next to the existing absolute gap. E8, E9c, E10 and E12.

##### Reporting
These go in the appendix as descriptive controls. Transport is presented as a repair that is checked empirically. The only guarantee is the label-loss lower bound of Prop. transport (a); the exact-transfer statement of (b) holds only for the population map under an exactly monotone change.

##### Outcomes (3 Oct; final rerun under source 25e8251b19b0, 32/32 ok)

1. **Oracles.**
   - At σ = 0 the oracle inverse is exact on all four datasets (max |Δcov| = 0.000).
   - At σ = 1 it misses by 0.06–0.08. The quantile map under an increasing change misses by about 0.02 on the frozen models.
   - So the useful target is E[V_A | V_B], not g⁻¹.
2. **Direction.**
   - A wrong-direction fit collapses to a constant forecast. On TriviaQA q the increasing fit gives 0.808 with singleton sets; the decreasing fit gives 0.905. In E10 at σ = 0 a wrong-direction fit misses by 0.10–0.11.
   - On the frozen models under the real reversal, both directions give near-full sets (0.94–1.00).
   - On PopQA Qwen the decreasing fit gives 0.713.
3. **Mid-rank map.** It agrees with the existing quantile map within 0.002 everywhere, and exactly on PopQA, including Qwen fwd with 15% ties.
4. **Permutation.** As before (E12): paired isotonic under-covers for Llama and Qwen at ρ = 1.
5. **Signed per-group gaps.**

   | Arm | TruthfulQA | PopQA |
   |---|---|---|
   | Quantile map, worst group | −0.04 to −0.10 | −0.06 to −0.21 |
   | Paired isotonic, worst group | ≥ −0.006 | Qwen −0.22 |
   | Recalibration, 60+60 labels | within 0.002 | within 0.006 |

**Reading:** label-free transport is a marginal repair, not a per-group one.

##### Amendment (4 Oct, before rerunning; from review round 4)

**1. Per-group scoring of the labelled reference.**
- **Bug:** `recal_reference` called `evaluate()` without the frozen groups, so its "worst group gap" was the marginal gap. The claim "labelled recalibration keeps every group within 0.006" was wrong.
- **Fix:** the reference is scored per group like every other arm.
- **Reporting:** worst-group gaps are reported net of the A→A arm's own worst-group gap. The worst-of-4 statistic is biased below zero even without a shift (A→A: −0.02 to −0.04).

**2. Honest split in E8/E10.**
- **Problem:** the Platt forecaster under A and the conformal threshold were fitted on the same labelled fold. That violates the honest-split rule of §2.4, so the split-conformal guarantee did not formally apply.
- **Fix:** the labelled fold is split in half, Platt on the first half and thresholds on the second; on TriviaQA the cal split is halved.
- **Consequence:** every E8, E9c and E10 number changes slightly. All are re-read from the rerun, and none is carried over.

No criterion changes. The pre-set checks of E8 and E10 are re-evaluated on the new outputs.

##### Outcomes after the amendment (4 Oct; final rerun under source 32d32a34ede1, 32/32 ok)

- **Same-procedure coverage.** Coverage is 0.919–0.922 on TruthfulQA and 0.909–0.910 on TriviaQA. The honest split leaves about 34 threshold points per group, so the thresholds are slightly conservative.
- **Per group, net of the A→A baseline.** No arm keeps every group (A→A's own worst group is already 0.02–0.04 short):

  | Arm | TruthfulQA | PopQA |
  |---|---|---|
  | Labelled 60+60 | 0.08–0.15 short | up to 0.06 short |
  | Quantile map | up to 0.05 short | up to 0.18 short |
  | Paired isotonic | keeps groups only with near-full sets | 0.19 short for Qwen |

  The earlier "60+60 within 0.006" was the marginal gap.
- **Transfer.**
  - Trained q reporter: 0.206 → 0.910 under paired isotonic, against A at 0.909. The label-loss mass is 0.013, plus a Hoeffding term of 0.012 at m = 10,647 and δ = 0.05.
  - Mistral on TruthfulQA: the quantile map takes 0.60–0.63 to 0.89–0.90.
  - PopQA quantile map: 0.84–0.95.
- **E10 checks:** PASS on all four datasets. The oracle is exact at σ = 0.

### `reports/postlock_analyses_note_2026-10-05.md`

#### Post-lock analyses: partition efficiency and probe baselines (dated note, 5 Oct 2026, written before running)

**Request (author):** "clone the repo and do the analysis", following an external plan. These analyses are added after the experiment lock (`reports/LOCK_2026-10-04.md`), so they are **post hoc**.

**How they respect the lock:**
- They do not rerun or modify any locked experiment.
- Code lives in `analyses/`, outside the hashed folders. Outputs go to `runs_postlock/`.
- Inputs are only the cached hidden states and reports already used: TruthfulQA Run 1 and PopQA-Elicit.
- The locked code is imported read-only for the tuned logistic, the partitions and the conformal quantile.
- `python -m experiments.run_all --popqa --check` must stay at 0 stale.

**External code:** `third_party/correctness-model-internals` (github.com/ivanvmoreno/correctness-model-internals @ aa7270c). Only its probe specification is reused: `StandardScaler` + `LogisticRegression(lbfgs, max_iter=1000, class_weight="balanced")` on the full state. No new extraction is needed, because the caches already hold candidate-conditioned states (question with the candidate answer).

##### A. Partition efficiency with a fixed score

**Question:** at the same label budget, do representation cells make conformal sets smaller while keeping coverage, compared with one cell or with bins of the report?

- **Splits:** the Granularity splits (TruthfulQA `[seed, 2525]`, PopQA-Elicit `[seed, 2527]`), 100 seeds.
  - The fit third is unlabelled and used for PCA, cells and report-bin edges.
  - The labelled third is halved: one half fits the score model, the other calibrates.
  - The test third is untouched.
- **Fixed score:** one correctness model per split and procedure, fitted once on the first labelled half. Two variants, each held fixed across partitions:
  - (i) R, Platt on the logit report;
  - (ii) D, tuned logistic on PCA-16 of the state plus the report.
  - Nonconformity is 1 − p̂(y).
- **Partitions:**
  - M = 1 (one global cell);
  - report-quantile bins, M ∈ {2, 4, 8}, edges from the fit third's reports;
  - farthest-first representation cells on PCA-16, M ∈ {2, 4, 8}.
  - Thresholds are per cell, with floor 20; below-floor cells return the full set.
- **Metrics:** coverage, mean set size, full-set rate, fallback mass (test mass in below-floor cells), worst-cell coverage. Means over seeds, averaged over the three procedures.
- **Reading:** descriptive. Representation cells are "useful" if they cut set size without coverage below 0.89 or a rise in fallback mass. Either outcome is reported.

##### B. Correctness-probe baselines

**Question:** does grouping remain useful against a learned internal-state probe on the same labels?

- **Setting:** the same splits and budgets as Granularity (TruthfulQA 60–272 labels, PopQA-Elicit 100–2,396), 100 seeds, Brier and log loss on the test third, averaged over procedures.
- **Arms** (all trained only on the n_lab labelled questions; labels spent on the probe count against the budget):

  | Arm | Model |
  |---|---|
  | R | report only |
  | P-their | full state, their spec (balanced weights) |
  | P16 | PCA-16 state, tuned and unweighted |
  | V+P | logistic on [logit V, logit P16], P16 cross-fitted (5-fold) on the labelled rows |
  | G4 | report plus 4 groups |
  | D | PCA-16 plus report, as in Granularity |

- **Inference:** Nadeau–Bengio intervals against R.
- **Reading:** descriptive. These arms are not added to the pre-declared Holm family.

##### Outcomes (5 Oct; 100 seeds each; runs_postlock/)

###### A. Partition efficiency
- **Coverage** is at least 0.90 for every arm.
- **PopQA (1,198 calibration points):** representation cells change set size by at most 0.006 against one cell; report bins enlarge sets slightly.
- **TruthfulQA (136 points):** every finer partition enlarges sets, because of floor fallback. Fallback mass is 15% for rep4, 35–41% for rep8 and 68% for bins8.
- **The score matters more than the partition:** D instead of R shrinks sets by 0.12 (PopQA) and 0.16 (TruthfulQA).
- **Verdict:** representation cells do not improve efficiency for a fixed score at these budgets.

###### B. Probe baselines
- **TruthfulQA:** the full-state probe (repo spec) is the best forecaster. Its Brier is −42 to −57 ×10⁻³ against R, with AUROC 0.81–0.83 (D: −32 to −36).
- **PopQA:** the same probe is badly miscalibrated (+69 to +127 ×10⁻³, because of balanced weights and an untuned penalty on 4,096 dimensions). P16 is mixed, and V+P is close to D.
- **Groups gain less than every representation-based predictor**, except the miscalibrated full probe on PopQA.

The paper has an appendix section ("Post-hoc analyses added after the experiment lock") and two body sentences.

## 7. Theory, novelty and audits


### `reports/theory.md`

#### Derivation and claim audit — HOLD

This is a project derivation, not the missing manuscript. “Proposition D,” its Section 5, the balanced-cell reading rules, and the original three functional definitions were absent from files-2.zip. The definitions below are explicit provisional choices. No NeurIPS-specific skill was installed.

##### T1. Conditional-on-count Beta law

Condition on the fit fold, which freezes the score function and partition, and on the cell's calibration count n. Assume independent, identically distributed calibration and future observations and a continuous score CDF F_j within cell j. Let t=1-alpha and k=ceil((n+1)t). If k<=n, the probability integral transform and uniform order-statistic density give

    C_j = F_j(S_(k)) ~ Beta(k,n+1-k),
    E C_j = k/(n+1),
    Var C_j = k(n+1-k)/[(n+1)^2(n+2)].

This follows by counting which n uniforms fall below a proposed order statistic: its density is n! / [(k-1)!(n-k)!] u^(k-1)(1-u)^(n-k). Integrating its first two moments gives the formulas above. If k=n+1, n=0, or n<floor, our threshold is +infinity and C_j=1 deterministically. Its variance is zero, but its squared error from t is alpha^2. With score ties, the exact Beta equality generally fails; rank-based coverage remains conservative under exchangeability.

Vovk's training-conditional analysis provides the tolerance-region context; the displayed Beta moments are derived here from order statistics, not attributed to a nonexistent named theorem in that paper. [Vovk (2012), primary source](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v25/vovk12.html).

##### T2. Cell MSCE does not contain within-cell approximation error

Write p_j=P(X in cell j | D_fit), and C_j=P(S<=q_j | cell j,D_fit,D_cal). Define cell MSCE=sum_j p_j(C_j-t)^2. Conditional on the vector of cell counts,

    E_Dcal MSCE = sum_j p_j [Var(C_j)+(E C_j-t)^2].

This identity is linearity of expectation and the variance-bias identity. It contains no variation of F_x within a cell. In the continuous no-floor case, approximately balanced n_j~n_cal/M gives a variance term of order M/n_cal. Flooring and discrete ranks can make this nonmonotone, but do not supply a geometric approximation term. Consequently a universal interior M*~n_cal^(d/(d+2)) is not justified for this functional.

##### T3. Exact pointwise decomposition and a conditional geometric bound

For a fixed calibration realization define h(x)=F_x(q_cell(x)). The orthogonal decomposition is

    E_X[(h(X)-t)^2]
      = E_X[(h(X)-E[h(X)|cell(X)])^2]
        + sum_j p_j(C_j-t)^2.

Proof: expand h-t=(h-C_j)+(C_j-t); the cross term vanishes conditional on each cell. The first term is within-cell heterogeneity at the *realized* calibrated threshold. It is not an independent bias term and generally changes with calibration.

If, uniformly in score threshold s, |F_x(s)-F_x'(s)| <= L ||x-x'||^beta for beta in (0,1], and all positive-mass cells have diameter at most K M^(-1/d), the first term is at most L^2 K^(2 beta) M^(-2 beta/d). Balanced population masses, growing counts, negligible floor activation, and controlled geometry are additional assumptions, not consequences of snapped k-means or empirical OT fitting. A bound alone does not establish an asymptotically tight risk expansion or the minimizer's rate.

X1 uses X uniform on [0,1]^d and S=(0.4+1.6 mean(X))*U for independent U uniform on [0,1]. The exact conditional CDF is clip(s/scale(x),0,1). Test CDF integration removes Bernoulli outcome noise but has finite-X integration error. The decomposition is exact for the empirical integration measure; population Beta predictions need not equal a single replicate.

##### T4. Surrogate balance and what it does not prove

For the *assumed surrogate* R(M)=A M^(-a)+B M^b/n_cal with positive A,B,a,b, differentiating yields

    M* = [a A n_cal/(b B)]^(1/(a+b)).

For pointwise squared coverage error, a=2 beta/d and b=1 give exponent d/(d+2 beta), hence d/(d+2) at beta=1. This reconciles the two expressions in the archive. Constants, integer M, finite fit sizes, unequal masses, floor activation, and slowly varying factors must still be addressed. The code rejects Mstar for functionals without a justified derivation.

##### Provisional other functionals

- `spread`: max_j C_j - min_j C_j over observed cells.
- `concentrated`: max_j (t-C_j)_+, equivalent to worst undercoverage over arbitrary mixtures supported on cells. This is not yet the manuscript's “concentrated-group” definition.

These are joint/extreme functionals. Exact one-cell Beta marginals do not imply a pointwise-MSCE exponent for either. Arbitrary subgroups inside cells have additional approximation effects. If the manuscript intends a different estimand, replace these definitions and redo the theory before gate release. Empty test cells remain undefined and are counted, not imputed as perfect coverage.

##### Frozen partitions, residuals, and top-k

The empirical transport objective is mean_i min_j(||X_i-e_j||^2-w_j)+mean_j w_j with fit-only X_i; its supergradient is 1/M minus empirical cell mass. The code records optimizer state and hard-assignment residuals. Empirical balance is not population balance. [Peyré, semi-discrete transport dual](https://www.gpeyre.com/ot4ml/myst/_build/html/semidiscrete-w1/).

Residual assignment picks the nearest exemplar whose fixed radius contains x, otherwise cell M. Radii must be fit-only; reusing calibration scores/points to learn the partition needs another independent split or a separate proof. The archive's “calibrated radius” phrase is insufficient to establish Proposition D.

Top-k neighborhoods overlap. The implemented diagnostic pools each calibration row once if its membership list intersects the query's list. Query-dependent pools are not a fixed disjoint partition, so the usual Mondrian proof does not transfer. k=1 is tested against ordinary partition calibration.

##### Gate policy recorded before X1

Tests must pass. X1 reports decomposition residuals, Beta-expectation discrepancies, seed-mean M* on a fixed grid, boundary minima, seed-bootstrap slope intervals, and jointly resampled slope differences. Eight seeds and a coarse grid are diagnostics, not decisive asymptotic evidence. A CI containing the proposed exponent is not equivalence evidence.

X1 remains HOLD until the actual functionals are supplied or a revised estimand is accepted, functional-specific claims are derived, and a prospectively chosen equivalence/power criterion is satisfied with adequate interior grid resolution. The current code deliberately cannot auto-pass this scientific gate. Do not edit a gate JSON to bypass it. Later-stage PASS means diagnostic completion only; `paper_status` remains HOLD pending review.

### `reports/lemma_diameter.md`

#### Lemma lem:diam — cell diameters for farthest-first exemplars (proof + numeric check)

Status: proof complete for farthest-first (Gonzalez) exemplars with nearest-exemplar
(Voronoi) cells. Not covered: power cells (fitted OT weights), the residual cell, and k-means
exemplars (see Section 5). Numeric check: `experiments/check_diameter.py` → `runs/p1_diameter/`.

Notation. $S=\operatorname{supp}P_X\subset\mathbb R^d$ is compact, $D=\operatorname{diam}S$, and $\omega_d$
is the volume of the unit ball. $D_{\rm fit}=\{X_1,\dots,X_n\}$ is i.i.d. $P_X$ with $n=n_{\rm fit}$.
$E_M=\{e_1,\dots,e_M\}\subset D_{\rm fit}$ are the exemplars.
$V_j=\{x\in S:\|x-e_j\|\le\|x-e_k\|\ \forall k\}$ is the population cell. Tie-breaking removes a
boundary from a cell, so it can only shrink it, and every bound below survives tie-breaking.

##### 1. Assumptions

**(G1) Density lower bound.** $P_X$ has a Lebesgue density $p\ge c>0$ on $S$.

**(G2) Regular support.** There are $\kappa\in(0,1]$ and $r_0>0$ with
$\mathrm{Vol}(B(x,r)\cap S)\ge\kappa\,\omega_d r^d$ for all $x\in S$ and $0<r\le r_0$.
This is the standard "$(c_0,r_0)$-regular set" condition of Audibert and Tsybakov (2007).
It holds:
- for any convex body $S$ with $\kappa\omega_d=\mathrm{Vol}(S)/D^d$ and $r_0=D$, because
  $x+\tfrac rD(S-x)\subset B(x,r)\cap S$;
- for $[0,1]^d$ with $\kappa=2^{-d}$ and $r_0=1$ (one orthant always fits);
- for sets satisfying an interior cone condition, and finite unions of such sets.

(G2) fails for supports with outward cusps. A thin spike carries little mass, yet a single cell
must stretch along it, so the regularity condition is genuinely needed.

(G1) and (G2) together give, for every $x\in S$ and $r>0$, with $a:=c\,\kappa\,\omega_d$:
$$P_X(B(x,r))\ \ge\ a\,\min(r,r_0)^d. \tag{1}$$

**(G3) Density upper bound** (needed only for the mass bounds in Section 3): $p\le\bar c$.

Gonzalez traversal works as follows. Pick $e_1\in D_{\rm fit}$ arbitrarily (in the code, at
random). Then set $e_{k+1}\in\arg\max_i d(X_i,E_k)$, with any tie rule. This is
`select_exemplars(..., method="voronoi")`.

##### 2. Lemma and proof

Let $C_1:=\max(2,D/r_0)$ and fix $s>1$. Define
$$\delta_n:=2\Big(\frac{s\log n}{a\,n}\Big)^{1/d},\qquad m(n):=\frac{n}{2^d\,s\,\log n},\qquad K:=2(C_1+1)\,a^{-1/d}.$$

**Lemma (cell diameters).** Assume (G1) and (G2), and let $n/\log n\ge s/(2^d a r_0^d)$.
Then there is an event $\Omega_n$ with
$$P(\Omega_n^c)\ \le\ \frac{2^d\,n^{1-s}}{s\log n}$$
such that on $\Omega_n$, for **every** $M\le m(n)$ (with $M<n$), every starting point and every
tie rule of the traversal,
$$\max_{j\le M}\operatorname{diam}V_j\ \le\ 2\big(r_M+\delta_n\big)\ \le\ K\,M^{-1/d}.$$
If $M\le\eta^d m(n)$ with $\eta\le1$, the constant improves to $K_\eta=2(C_1+\eta)a^{-1/d}$.
As $M\log n/n\to0$ it tends to $K_\infty=2C_1a^{-1/d}$.

For $X\sim U[0,1]^d$ we have $a=2^{-d}\omega_d$ and $C_1=\max(2,\sqrt d)$:

| $d$ | $K$ (lemma) | $K_\infty$ |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 6 | 4 |
| 2 | $6/\sqrt{\pi/4}\approx 6.77$ | 4.51 |

With $s=2$, $m(n)=n/(2^{d+1}\log n)$ and $P(\Omega_n^c)\le 2^{d-1}/(n\log n)$.

**Step 1 (deterministic separation of the traversal).**
Let $\rho_k:=\max_i d(X_i,E_k)=d(e_{k+1},E_k)$. Because $E_k$ grows with $k$, $\rho_k$ is
non-increasing. For $i<j\le M+1$ we get $d(e_i,e_j)\ge d(e_j,E_{j-1})=\rho_{j-1}\ge\rho_M$. So the
$M+1$ points $e_1,\dots,e_{M+1}\in S$ are pairwise at distance at least $r_M:=\rho_M$. This is the
property behind the 2-approximation to $k$-center: $r_M\le2\,\mathrm{OPT}_M(D_{\rm fit})$.

The open balls $B(e_i,r_M/2)$ are therefore disjoint. By (1), each has mass at least
$a\min(r_M/2,r_0)^d$, and the masses sum to at most 1.
- If $r_M/2\le r_0$, then $r_M\le2(a(M+1))^{-1/d}$.
- Otherwise $(M+1)a r_0^d\le1$, so $r_0\le (a(M+1))^{-1/d}$ and
  $r_M\le D\le (D/r_0)(a(M+1))^{-1/d}$.

In both cases
$$r_M\ \le\ C_1\,(a(M+1))^{-1/d}\ \le\ C_1\,a^{-1/d}M^{-1/d}. \tag{2}$$
This holds surely, for every $M<n$ at once, and needs no probability.

**Step 2 (the sample is a $\delta_n$-net of $S$).**
Set $\varepsilon=\delta_n/2$. Take a maximal $\varepsilon$-separated set $\{z_k\}\subset S$. The balls
$B(z_k,\varepsilon/2)$ are disjoint and each has mass at least $a(\varepsilon/2)^d$; the assumption on $n$
ensures $\varepsilon/2=\delta_n/4\le r_0$. So there are at most $N\le 2^d/(a\varepsilon^d)$ points.

Let $\Omega_n$ be the event that every ball $B(z_k,\varepsilon)$ contains a point of $D_{\rm fit}$. Each such
ball has mass at least $a\varepsilon^d=a\delta_n^d/2^d=s\log n/n$. Hence
$$P(\Omega_n^c)\le N(1-s\log n/n)^n\le \frac{2^d n}{s\log n}\,n^{-s}.$$
On $\Omega_n$, any $x\in S$ is within $\varepsilon$ of some $z_k$ (by maximality), and that $z_k$ is within
$\varepsilon$ of a sample point. So $\sup_{x\in S}d(x,D_{\rm fit})\le\delta_n$.

**Step 3 (from the sample to the population covering radius).**
For $x\in S$, let $X_i$ be its nearest sample point. Then
$$d(x,E_M)\le d(x,X_i)+d(X_i,E_M)\le\delta_n+r_M.$$
So $R_M:=\sup_{x\in S}d(x,E_M)\le r_M+\delta_n$ on $\Omega_n$.

**Step 4 (from covering radius to diameter).**
If $x\in V_j$, then $\|x-e_j\|=d(x,E_M)\le R_M$, so $V_j\subset B(e_j,R_M)$ and
$\operatorname{diam}V_j\le2R_M$. Now use $\delta_n\le a^{-1/d}M^{-1/d}$, which is equivalent to
$M\le 1/(a\delta_n^d)=m(n)$, together with (2):
$$\operatorname{diam}V_j\le 2(C_1+1)a^{-1/d}M^{-1/d}=K M^{-1/d}.$$
The bound holds for every cell, not just the positive-mass ones. $\square$

Remarks.
- The randomness of $e_1$ and the dependence of $E_M$ on $D_{\rm fit}$ do not matter. Step 1 is
  deterministic, and $\Omega_n$ is a property of $D_{\rm fit}$ alone.
- Since $\rho_k$ is monotone, the bound holds simultaneously for the nested family $E_1\subset E_2\subset\cdots$.
- **The range $M\lesssim n/\log n$ is sharp up to constants.** The largest empty ball of the
  sample inside $S$ has radius of order $(\log n/n)^{1/d}$ w.h.p. (maximal spacings: Janson 1987;
  Penrose 2023 for $d\ge1$ — *verify the exact references before citing*). The centre of that ball is at
  least its radius away from every exemplar. So $\max_j\operatorname{diam}V_j\gtrsim(\log n/n)^{1/d}$, which exceeds
  $KM^{-1/d}$ once $M\gg n/\log n$.

##### 3. Mass bounds and Theorem B with explicit $n_{\rm fit}$ dependence

**Lemma (cell masses; needs G3).** Write $m'(n):=\dfrac{a}{2^d\bar c\,\omega_d}\,m(n)$ and
$b:=\dfrac{a}{4^d\bar c\,\omega_d}=\dfrac{c\kappa}{4^d\bar c}$.
On $\Omega_n$, for $2\le M\le m'(n)$:
$$\frac{b}{M}\ \le\ p_j:=P_X(V_j)\ \le\ \frac{\bar c\,\omega_dK^d}{2^d M}.$$

Proof.
- *Upper bound.* $V_j\subset B(e_j,KM^{-1/d}/2)$.
- *Lower bound, part 1.* $S$ is covered by $M$ balls of radius $R_M$, so
  $M\omega_dR_M^d\ge\mathrm{Vol}(S)\ge1/\bar c$.
- *Lower bound, part 2.* On $\Omega_n$ we then get
  $r_M\ge R_M-\delta_n\ge\tfrac12(\bar c\omega_dM)^{-1/d}$, using $M\le m'(n)$.
- *Lower bound, part 3.* Exemplars are $\ge r_M$ apart (Step 1), so $V_j\supset B(e_j,r_M/2)\cap S$.
  By (1), $p_j\ge a(r_M/4)^d\ge b/M$; the case $r_M/2>r_0$ gives an even larger bound. $\square$

For $U[0,1]^2$: $b=1/64$ and $m'(n)=m(n)/16$. These constants are conservative.

**Theorem B (farthest-first form).** Assume the following:
- Assumption B(i);
- (G1)–(G3);
- Gonzalez exemplars on $D_{\rm fit}$ with nearest-exemplar cells;
- $D_{\rm cal}$ independent of $D_{\rm fit}$;
- $t=1-\alpha$, and a floor $n_{\min}\ge t/\alpha$, so that $k=\lceil(n+1)t\rceil\le n$ above the floor.

Take $2\le M\le\min\{m'(n_{\rm fit}),\,b\,n_{\rm cal}/(2n_{\min})\}$ and $n_{\rm fit}/\log n_{\rm fit}\ge s/(2^dar_0^d)$. Then
$$
\E[R_{\rm pt}]\ \le\ L^2K^{2\beta}M^{-2\beta/d}\;+\;t(1-t)\frac{M}{n_{\rm cal}+1}\;+\;\frac{3M^2}{b\,(n_{\rm cal}+1)^2}\;+\;\alpha^2e^{-b\,n_{\rm cal}/(8M)}\;+\;\frac{2^d\,n_{\rm fit}^{1-s}}{s\log n_{\rm fit}}.
$$
The five terms are, in order:
1. quantisation;
2. Beta variance;
3. order-statistic bias plus the $O(n^{-2})$ part of the variance;
4. floor (below-floor cells);
5. failure of $\Omega_n$.

Proof sketch (each step is elementary).
- *Term 1.* On $\Omega_n$ the diameter lemma and B(i) give
  $|h(x)-C_j|\le\sup_{x'\in V_j}\sup_s|F_x(s)-F_{x'}(s)|\le L\,\mathrm{diam}_j^\beta$.
  This is uniform in the threshold, so it holds at the realised thresholds.
- *Term 5.* Off $\Omega_n$, $R_{\rm pt}\le1$.
- *Term 2.* Condition on $D_{\rm fit}$ and use Prop. B0. Above the floor,
  $\mathrm{Var}(C_j)\le t(1-t)/(n_j+2)+1/((n_j+1)(n_j+2))$. With $n_j\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n_{\rm cal},p_j)$,
  $\E[1/(n_j+1)]\le1/((n_{\rm cal}+1)p_j)$. Summing $p_j\cdot$ over $j$ gives
  $t(1-t)M/(n_{\rm cal}+1)$. **This term needs no balance.**
- *Term 3.* Uses $(k/(n+1)-t)^2\le(n+1)^{-2}$,
  $\E[1/((n_j+1)(n_j+2))]\le1/((n_{\rm cal}+1)(n_{\rm cal}+2)p_j^2)$ and $p_j\ge b/M$.
- *Term 4.* Uses the Chernoff bound $P(n_j<n_{\rm cal}p_j/2)\le e^{-n_{\rm cal}p_j/8}$ together with
  $n_{\min}\le n_{\rm cal}p_j/2$.

$M=1$ is trivial: cell = $S$, and diam $\le D\le K$.

Consequences.
- **Rate.** Take $M\asymp n_{\rm cal}^{d/(d+2\beta)}$. Then term 3 is $O(n_{\rm cal}^{-4\beta/(d+2\beta)})$ and
  term 4 is exponentially small, so terms 1–2 give $O(n_{\rm cal}^{-2\beta/(d+2\beta)})$. This needs
  two things:
  - (a) $n_{\rm cal}^{d/(d+2\beta)}\le m'(n_{\rm fit})$, i.e. $n_{\rm fit}/\log n_{\rm fit}\gtrsim n_{\rm cal}^{d/(d+2\beta)}$;
  - (b) term 5 is negligible. If $n_{\rm fit}\ge n_{\rm cal}^\gamma$, choose
    $s\ge1+2\beta/(\gamma(d+2\beta))$. A larger $s$ shrinks $m$ only by a constant factor.
- **Conditional version.** Equivalently, with probability $\ge1-2^dn_{\rm fit}^{1-s}/(s\log n_{\rm fit})$ over $D_{\rm fit}$, the bound
  holds conditionally on $D_{\rm fit}$ without term 5.
- **"No floor activation"** in the current theorem statement can be replaced by term 4. The
  floor is the only below-floor effect; it costs at most $\alpha^2$ per unit of affected mass.
- **Without (G3).** Drop the mass lemma. Term 2 still holds with no balance needed. Terms 3–4
  then need an assumed lower bound $\min_jp_j\ge b/M$, or else must be replaced by
  "no floor activation" as in the current text.
- **Conjecture conj:B.** The mass lemma also gives the *geometric* half of the lower bound: every
  cell contains a ball of radius $\ge\frac14(\bar c\omega_dM)^{-1/d}$. Under a non-degeneracy condition
  (e.g. $\|\nabla_xF_x(s)\|\ge\lambda$ near the quantile), this makes the within-cell variance of $h$
  $\gtrsim\lambda^2M^{-2/d}$. The remaining gap is that $h$ is evaluated at the *realised* threshold. I did
  not close this, so the statement stays a conjecture.
- **Remark rem:drift** is unaffected.

##### 4. Suggested replacement text for the paper (for the integrating agent)

Lemma lem:diam: *"Assume $P_X$ has density $\ge c$ on a compact $S$ with
$\mathrm{Vol}(B(x,r)\cap S)\ge\kappa\omega_dr^d$ for $x\in S$, $r\le r_0$ (e.g. a convex body or $[0,1]^d$).
Let exemplars be the first $M$ points of a farthest-first traversal of $D_{\rm fit}$, and let cells be
nearest-exemplar cells. With $a=c\kappa\omega_d$ and $s>1$: with probability at least
$1-2^dn_{\rm fit}^{1-s}/(s\log n_{\rm fit})$, simultaneously for all
$M\le n_{\rm fit}/(2^ds\log n_{\rm fit})$, every cell has diameter at most $KM^{-1/d}$, where
$K=2(\max(2,\mathrm{diam}S/r_0)+1)a^{-1/d}$."*

Theorem B then uses the five-term display above. The phrase "farthest-first is a 2-approximation"
can stay as intuition, but the proof only uses the separation property (Step 1).

##### 5. k-means vs farthest-first — honest assessment

**What X1 actually ran.** X1 uses k-means snapped exemplars:
- `experiments/x1_synthetic.py::run(... method="kmeans", rule="voronoi")`, and
- `mondrian/exemplars.py`: sklearn KMeans with `n_init=10`, followed by a one-to-one Hungarian snap to $D_{\rm fit}$.

So the lemma above does **not** cover X1 as run.

**Why there is no clean k-means lemma.**
- sklearn returns a local optimum of the *empirical* distortion. Lloyd fixed points are centroidal
  Voronoi tessellations, and for $d\ge2$ such tessellations can have cells of diameter $\asymp1$.
  For example, $M$ parallel strips of width $1/M$ on $[0,1]^2$ form a CVT (a Lloyd fixed point) with
  cell diameter $\ge1\gg M^{-1/2}$.
- In practice `n_init=10` with k-means++ seeding avoids such configurations. Still, no deterministic
  separation property holds, and k-means++ guarantees are only in expectation and only on distortion.
- A rigorous k-means version would need *globally optimal* population quantizers. Graf, Luschgy and
  Pagès (Ann. Probab. 2012, "local quantization behaviour") show cell radius $\asymp M^{-1/d}$ and mass
  $\asymp 1/M$ for optimal quantizers of densities bounded below on convex supports. *Check the
  exact hypotheses before citing.*
- That version would also need an empirical-to-population stability argument and a bound on the
  snapping displacement. The Hungarian snap is one-to-one, so a single centre's move is not
  automatically bounded by $\delta_n$.
- This amounts to assumptions about the optimiser that X1 cannot verify.

**Recommendation.**
- State Lemma lem:diam and Theorem B for farthest-first, where the proof is complete and the
  constants are explicit.
- Add a farthest-first arm to X1: `method="voronoi"`, already implemented, with the same grid, seeds
  and $n_{\rm fit}=4000$. The gate claim should then rest on that arm.
- Keep k-means as a secondary arm. Describe it as "empirically satisfies the diameter condition,
  see check_diameter; not covered by the lemma."
- Do not claim the theorem for k-means.

The numeric check below shows k-means cells behave much like farthest-first cells at this $n_{\rm fit}$.
The swap is therefore expected to change X1 little, but that needs to be run, not assumed.

##### 6. Numeric check (`python -m experiments.check_diameter`, outputs in `runs/p1_diameter/`)

**Setup.**
- $X\sim U[0,1]^d$, $n_{\rm fit}=4000$, 10 seeds.
- M grid as in X1: $\{1,\dots,190\}$.
- Population Voronoi cells clipped to $[0,1]^d$ are computed **exactly**:
  - $d=1$: midpoints between neighbouring exemplars;
  - $d=2$: half-plane clipping of the square, with diameter = max vertex distance.
- A Monte-Carlo cross-check (200k uniform points, convex hull per cell) agrees to within 0.5–3%.
- Slopes come from regressing log of the seed-mean max-diameter on log M.
- $\hat K=\max_{\rm seeds}\max_j\mathrm{diam}_j\cdot M^{1/d}$.

| arm | slope (M≥4) [seed sd] | slope (all M) | covering-radius slope | $\hat K$ max over M, seeds | lemma $K$ / $K_\infty$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $d=1$ farthest-first | −1.00 [0.03] | −0.97 | −1.02 | 1.91 | 6 / 4 |
| $d=1$ k-means snapped | −0.91 [0.01] | −0.92 | −0.89 | 1.55 | (n/a) |
| $d=2$ farthest-first | −0.54 [0.01] | −0.51 | −0.56 | 2.29 | 6.77 / 4.51 |
| $d=2$ k-means snapped | −0.46 [0.004] | −0.48 | −0.43 | 1.94 | (n/a) |

**Reading the table.**
- *Farthest-first.* It matches $-1/d$, with $\hat K$ flat in $M$:

  | $d$ | $\hat K$ range | lemma $K$ |
  |---|---|---|
  | 1 | 1.5–1.9 | 6 |
  | 2 | 1.75–2.3 | 6.77 |

  The constants in the lemma are conservative by a factor of about 3.
- *k-means.* The slopes are slightly shallower than $-1/d$, and $\hat K$ creeps upward with $M$:

  | $d$ | $\hat K$ from $M=4$ | to $M=190$ |
  |---|---|---|
  | 1 | 1.08 | 1.55 |
  | 2 | 1.44 | 1.94 |

  This is consistent with sampling fluctuation of the empirical optimum when cells hold about
  $n_{\rm fit}/M\approx20$ points (the max over $M$ cells grows). It is a finite-$n_{\rm fit}$ effect that the
  farthest-first bound controls deterministically.
- *Both methods.* In absolute terms both stay below $2M^{-1/d}$ on the whole grid.
- *Range caveat.* At $n_{\rm fit}=4000$, $s=2$, the lemma's guaranteed range is $m(n)\approx120$ ($d=1$) and
  $\approx60$ ($d=2$). Larger X1 grid points are covered empirically but not by the stated constants.

  conflict-of-interest data are collected at the abstract stage, so a paper with no registered abstract
  cannot be submitted. **Check OpenReview to confirm that an abstract was registered by 29 Sep.**
- Page limit: 8 pages, not counting references, the AI Use Statement, the reproducibility checklist or
  appendices. Venue: OpenReview, group `aistats.org/AISTATS/2027/Conference`. Reviews are released on
  16 Nov 2026 and decisions on 20 Jan 2027.

---

##### 1. Per-claim verdicts (short)

| Claim | Verdict | Decisive prior work |
|---|---|---|
| Thm A (per-cell validity, upper bound) | Already known (the paper labels it standard) | Vovk 2012 Prop. 3; Vovk et al. 2005; Ding et al. 2023 Prop. 1 |
| Prop M-suff (stage measurability) | Already known / folklore | Vovk 2012 (inductive taxonomy K((z_1..z_m), z)); Bao et al. 2024 Thm 1; Jin & Ren 2025 §1.1 |
| Prop M-fail (outcome selection) | Already known mechanism; the LLM "answerable set" framing is new but trivial | Jin & Ren 2025; Bao et al. 2024; Wang 2026 (retained-law transfer); Kumar et al. 2023 Fig. 8 (empirical) |
| Rem rem:vc (a)-(c) | (a),(c) known; (b) a practical caveat, not novel theory | Ding et al. 2023 Props 1-3 (cluster vs class conditional, KS bridge); Cherian, Gibbs, Candès 2024 (coverage conditional on bins of a confidence level α(X)) |
| Prop B0 (cell MSCE depends only on counts) | Partially known: the per-cell Beta law, mean and variance are published verbatim; the aggregation and its interpretation are new but a one-line corollary | Vovk 2012 App. A (Beta via tolerance regions); Ding et al. 2023 §1.2 (exact Beta, mean, variance) |
| Prop decomp (pointwise = quantisation + cell) | Known in form (orthogonal / Pythagorean decomposition) | Same algebra as Sun, Song, Hero 2023 Prop. 1 and the Murphy 1973 partition |
| Thm B rate, M* ~ n^{d/(d+2β)} | Already known in substance for localized conformal; the hard-partition/Mondrian version with exact Beta variance is a minor variant | Conrad et al. 2026 (arXiv 2608.06206) Thm 3 and eq. (19)-(20); Min, Peng, Zou 2026 Table 1; Lei & Wasserman 2014 (partition local conformal); classical partitioning regression |
| Rem rem:drift (local-exponent slope) | Appears new, but it is an elementary implicit-function calculation | Nothing found; formula checked below |
| Prop G (Brier = irreducible + quantisation + estimation; bin count) | Already known | Sun, Song, Hero NeurIPS 2023 Prop. 1 + Thm 1 (B* ~ n^{1/3}); Murphy 1973; Kumar, Liang, Ma 2019 Prop. D.4; Gupta & Ramdas 2021; Futami & Fujisawa 2024 |

##### 2. Paper-by-paper notes

###### 2.1 Conformal: conditional, Mondrian and selection

**Vovk, V. (2012). Conditional validity of inductive conformal predictors. ACML, PMLR 25:475-490.
arXiv 1209.2673.** (PMLR page verified.)
- Proves: Prop. 3 says that for an inductive m-taxonomy K((z_1..z_m), z), a category computed from the
  proper training set and the example, the error probability conditional on the test category is ≤ ε.
  Label-conditional validity is the special case K = y. Props 2a/2b give PAC training-conditional
  validity. App. A shows the coverage of a classical tolerance region is Beta((1-ε)(n+1), ε(n+1)).
  Prop. 4 shows object-conditional validity is impossible.
- vs **Thm A / M-suff**: Thm A is exactly Prop. 3 combined with a taxonomy frozen on D_fit. M-suff
  restates the requirement that the taxonomy be computable from what is observed. Vovk allows the
  category to depend on y, and is valid *within* that category, which is the paper's own remark. Folklore.
- vs **B0**: App. A supplies the Beta law that B0 aggregates.

**Ding, T., Angelopoulos, A. N., Bates, S., Jordan, M. I., Tibshirani, R. J. (2023). Class-conditional
conformal prediction with many classes. NeurIPS 36. arXiv 2306.09335.** (Read.)
- §1.2 states verbatim: "the exact distribution of the CLASSWISE class-conditional coverage of class y
  given a fixed calibration set is (Vovk, 2012; Angelopoulos and Bates, 2023) Beta(k_α^y, |I_y|+1-k_α^y)",
  with mean k/(n+1) and variance k(n+1-k)/((n+1)^2(n+2)) ≈ α(1-α)/(n+2).
- Prop. 1: cluster-conditional coverage. Prop. 2: class-conditional coverage if the clustering is the
  oracle. Prop. 3: if within-cluster KS distance ≤ ε, class coverage is ≥ 1-α-ε. The method fits the
  clusters on a split D_1 that is disjoint from the calibration split D_2. Figure 1 gives the
  granularity/variance trade-off ("Low variance but insufficient granularity" vs "high variance").
- vs **B0**: every term of B0's displayed formula is in Ding §1.2. What is new is only the sum
  Σ_j p_j[·], the observation that it is free of the law of S|X, and the ≈ t(1-t)M/n approximation.
  Ding's CovGap is measured on *classes*, not on the method's own clusters, so it avoids the blindness
  that B0 formalises.
- vs **rem:vc(c)**: "bin-conditional does not imply latent-conditional" is the gap between Ding's
  Prop. 1 and Prop. 2. Ding's Prop. 3 KS bridge is the standard quantitative form.
- vs **Thm B**: Ding chooses M by heuristic (M = ⌊γñ/2⌋) and has no rate. Thm B is not in Ding.

**Jin, Y., Ren, Z. (2025). Confidence on the focal: conformal prediction with selection-conditional
coverage. JRSSB 87(4):1239-1259. arXiv 2403.03868.** (Read.)
- Proves exact selection-conditional coverage P(Y ∈ Ĉ | j ∈ Ŝ, Ŝ ∈ 𝒮) ≥ 1-α (JOMI, which builds a
  "reference set") for any selection rule that is permutation-invariant in the calibration data.
  §1.1: "given a selection event, the calibration data are no longer exchangeable with the test point,
  leading to violation of the coverage guarantee". The paper also notes that conditional coverage
  implies (2) "if the selection rule only depends on test features".
- vs **M-suff**: covariate-measurable selection applied to both calibration and test units preserves
  validity. This is folklore, and Jin & Ren (and Bao et al. Thm 1) state it in more generality.
- vs **M-fail**: Jin & Ren's selection is on test features or calibration labels, not on the test
  *outcome*. M-fail calibrates on {Y=1} and deploys on everything, which is a calibration/test law
  mismatch rather than selective inference. The (1-p)t gap in the toy model is trivial arithmetic.

**Bao, Y., Huo, Y., Ren, H., Zou, C. (2024). Selective conformal inference with false
coverage-statement rate control. Biometrika 111(3):727-742. arXiv 2301.00584.** (Read; venue verified.)
- Thm 1 (SCOP): apply the same selection rule (threshold τ̂ on T_i = g(X_i)) to the calibration set and
  calibrate on the selected calibration points. Then P(Y_j ∉ PI_j | j ∈ Ŝ_u) ≤ α and FCR ≤ α, provided
  τ̂ is exchangeable in {T_i}.
- vs **M-suff**: M-suff's clause "selecting units by an I_t-measurable event preserves exchangeability
  provided the test unit is subjected to the same event" is Bao et al. Thm 1 with a fixed threshold.
  Already known.

**Wang, C. (2026). When does trimming help conformal prediction? A retained-law diagnostic under
calibration contamination. arXiv 2605.06204.** (Read.)
- Prop. 1: if calibration uses the retained law R = P*(·|S ≤ t*), then for any target P_0,
  P(A ≤ τ̂) ≥ 1-α-sup_t (F_R(t)-F_{P_0}(t))_+. Thm 1 gives the exact finite-sample identity. The paper
  explicitly warns that "response-dependent filtering often couples retention with the nonconformity
  score".
- vs **M-fail**: M-fail is the special case in which the retention event is {Y=1}. Its gap
  (1-p)t = F_R(q)-F_P(q) is exactly this transfer gap. Cite it as the general statement.

**Gibbs, I., Cherian, J. J., Candès, E. J. (2025). Conformal prediction with conditional guarantees.
JRSSB 87(4):1100-1126. arXiv 2305.12616.** (Venue verified by search; content known through
Cherian et al. 2024 and Min et al. 2026.)
- Gives coverage over a finite-dimensional function class F, which includes any finite collection of
  groups. Fixed bins are a special case. No cell-count/rate trade-off of the Thm B type.

**Barber, Candès, Ramdas, Tibshirani (2021), IMA** and **Lei & Wasserman (2014)**: impossibility of
X-conditional coverage. Background only.

**Lei, J., Wasserman, L. (2014). Distribution-free prediction bands for non-parametric regression.
JRSSB 76(1):71-96. doi 10.1111/rssb.12021. arXiv 1203.5422 (titled "Distribution free prediction
bands").** (Read.)
- Def. 2 (local validity) is coverage conditional on X ∈ A_j for a partition with diameter ≤ δ. Prop. 5
  gives finite-sample local validity of per-bin conformal (a Mondrian partition on X). Thm 9 and
  Lemma 10: with cubic bins of width w_n ≍ r_n = (log n/n)^{β/(β(d+2)+1)}, the band converges to the
  oracle at rate r_n and is asymptotically conditionally valid. Thm 12 shows the rate is minimax.
- vs **Thm B**: this is the origin of "partition-based local conformal with a shrinking cell width".
  Their rate concerns set efficiency (symmetric difference to the oracle band) under smoothness in both
  x and y. It is not a mean-squared coverage gap, so the exponents differ. The *idea* that cells shrink
  at a rate set by bias-variance balance is theirs.

**Conrad, A., Isaev, R., Belomestny, D., Moulines, E., Samsonov, S. (2026). Beyond marginal validity:
finite-sample guarantees for localized conformal prediction. arXiv 2608.06206.** (Read.) **The decisive
paper for Thm B.**
- Assumption A2(S) is that the conditional score CDF is β-Hölder in x in Kolmogorov distance, which is
  the same as the paper's Ass. B(i). Thm 3 says that with probability ≥ 1-δ, uniformly over
  x ∈ B(x̃,h), |cond. coverage - (1-α)| ≲ A^cal_{n,h}(δ) + h^β with A^cal ≍ (log(4/δ)/(n p_min h^d))^{1/2}.
  Eq. (19)-(20): the balanced bandwidth is h* = (log(4n)/(n p_min))^{1/(2β+d)}, giving "the classical
  pointwise nonparametric rate n^{-β/(2β+d)}". They also run a bandwidth bias-variance simulation with
  fitted slopes of log h*(n).
- Translation: M ≍ h^{-d} gives M* ≍ n^{d/(2β+d)}, and the squared gap is n^{-2β/(2β+d)}. **This is
  exactly Thm B's rate.** Their proof decomposition (localization bias L_S(2h)^β plus calibration error
  of the empirical quantile) has the same structure as Thm B's sketch. Their finite-grid slopes also
  deviate from theory (−0.285 vs −0.25 at β=0.5), which is the phenomenon rem:drift explains.
- Thm B is new only in being a hard-partition (Mondrian) version, using exemplar cells fitted on D_fit,
  an L2-in-expectation form, and the exact Beta variance instead of a DKW bound. Rate novelty must not
  be claimed.

**Min, Y., Peng, L., Zou, C. (2026). A unified theory of conditional coverage in conformal prediction
with applications. arXiv 2605.11602.** (Read.)
- Thm 2 splits conditional miscoverage into score-estimation, finite-sample calibration and intrinsic
  conditional-mismatch terms. Table 1 gives LCP/RLCP rates of O((nh^d)^{-1/2}+h), and BatchGCP
  (group-conditional) O(n^{-1/2}).
- vs **Prop decomp / Thm B**: the "intrinsic mismatch" and "calibration" terms are Thm B's quantisation
  and Beta-variance terms. Cite it as the general framework.

**Hore, R., Barber, R. F. (2025). Conformal prediction with local weights: randomization enables robust
guarantees. JRSSB 87(2):549-578.** (Venue verified by search; content via Conrad et al. and
Min et al.) RLCP is the object analysed by Conrad et al.

**Berthier, L., Shokry, A., Moreaud, M., Ramelet, G., Dieuleveut, A. (2026). Self-organized conformal
prediction: reducing regional coverage gaps with unsupervised group discovery. arXiv 2606.29403.**
(Read.)
- Groups are learned by an SOM *without calibration labels* (a frozen, learned taxonomy). Thm 3.6 gives
  exact cell-conditional validity. Thm 3.8 adds a KS bias for pooled neighbourhoods. They explicitly
  name the granularity bias/variance trade-off, and they warn that "evaluation on a method's own
  partition could favor it by design", so they audit on external k-means partitions.
- vs the exemplar-cell setup and **B0**: this is the closest *learned-taxonomy* precedent and should be
  cited. B0 supplies the theory behind their audit warning, which is new as a stated result but should
  be presented as a corollary or remark.

**Gao, Z., Liu, P., Yang, A. Y., Belbahri, M., Cresswell, J. C., Asgharian, M. (2026). On the burden of
achieving fairness in conformal prediction. arXiv 2605.14260.** (Read.)
- Thm 1 is a conservation law Σ_g p_g ε_g(q) = 0 for a pooled threshold. Thm 2 gives
  Var(ε_G) ≥ m_eff² Var(q_G). The analysis is explicitly population-level, "separat[ing] the structural
  effect of group heterogeneity from finite-sample calibration noise".
- vs **Prop C (lossless coarsening)** and the quantisation term: Prop C's "merge iff q_j = q_k" is the
  two-group case of their conservation law. Cite them. There is no rate in M.

**Bian, M., Barber, R. F. (2023). Training-conditional coverage for distribution-free predictive
inference. EJS 17(2):2044-2066. arXiv 2205.03647.** (Read.)
- Thm 1 (from Vovk 2012 Prop. 2a): split conformal gives α_P(D_n) ≤ α + sqrt(log(1/δ)/(2n_1)) with
  probability ≥ 1-δ. Full conformal and jackknife+ have no such guarantee.
- vs **B0 / Thm B**: B0 and Thm B are statements about the calibration-conditional coverage C_j, so they
  belong to this training-conditional line. A per-cell PAC version would follow from their Lemma 1. Cite
  it when C_j is introduced.

###### 2.2 Conformal for LLMs

**Mohri, C., Hashimoto, T. (2024). Language models with conformal factuality guarantees. arXiv
2402.10978 (ICML 2024; the venue was not checked against the proceedings page).** (Read.)
- Thm 4.1 gives marginal factuality with a back-off over sub-claims. Scores include a verbalised "GPT-4
  confidence" and a frequency (self-consistency) score. There is no stratification and no conditional
  guarantee.

**Cherian, J. J., Gibbs, I., Candès, E. J. (2024). Large language model validity via enhanced conformal
prediction methods. NeurIPS 2024. arXiv 2406.09714.** (Read.)
- Thm 3.2 (level-adaptive) says that, simultaneously over groups G and sub-intervals I of a data-adaptive
  level α(X), P(output factual | α_{n+1} ∈ I, P_{n+1} ∈ G) = E[α_{n+1} | ·]. Fig. 6 shows split
  conformal (Mohri & Hashimoto) mis-covering across popularity bins.
- vs **rem:vc / confidence bins**: this is the closest LLM precedent for "coverage conditional on a
  confidence bin". Their α(·) is fitted on a separate split, which is the D_fit discipline. It must be
  cited. They do not analyse stage measurability or bin count.

**Quach, V., Fisch, A., Schuster, T., Yala, A., Sohn, J. H., Jaakkola, T., Barzilay, R. (2024).
Conformal language modeling. ICLR 2024. arXiv 2306.10193.** (Header read.) Gives marginal/PAC set
coverage via LTT and no stratification.

**Abbasi-Yadkori, Y., Kuzborskij, I., Stutz, D., György, A., Fisch, A., Doucet, A., Beloshapka, I.,
Weng, W.-H., Yang, Y.-Y., Szepesvári, C., Cemgil, A. T., Tomasev, N. (2024). Mitigating LLM
hallucinations via conformal abstention. arXiv 2405.01563.** (Read.) Abstention is a threshold on a
self-evaluation match-count score calibrated by CRC/RCPS, with a marginal risk bound and no bins. It is
an example of a stage-1 (answer-computed) decision.

**Kumar, B., Lu, C., Gupta, G., Palepu, A., Bellamy, D., Raskar, R., Beam, A. (2023). Conformal
prediction with large language models for multi-choice question answering. ICML 2023 Workshop
(Neural Conversational AI TEACH). arXiv 2305.18404.** (Read.) Fig. 6 reports set-size-stratified
coverage. Fig. 8 shows coverage loss when calibrating on one subject and testing on another (up to
about −7%), which is an empirical precedent for calibration/test category mismatch (M-fail).

No paper was found that (i) bins LLM *verbalized* confidence into Mondrian cells with a stage-measurability
analysis, or (ii) studies how many confidence bins to use for conformal coverage. Search used alphaXiv
discover with the keywords Mondrian, verbalized confidence, abstention and confidence bins, and
returned only 2026 papers. The closest is a hierarchical group-conditional CRC paper
(arXiv 2607.24562, title only, not read). The LLM application framing is therefore the most defensible
novelty, not the theory.

###### 2.3 Binning / recalibration and bin count

**Sun, Z., Song, D., Hero, A. (2023). Minimum-risk recalibration of classifiers. NeurIPS 2023
(spotlight). arXiv 2305.10886.** (Read.) **The decisive paper for Prop G.**
- Eq. (2): MSE(f) = Var[Y] − Var(E[Y|f(X)]) + E[(f(X)−E[Y|f(X)])²].
- Prop. 1: recalibration risk R(h) = E[(h∘f − E[Y|f])²] = R_cal + R_sha, where
  R_sha = E[(E[Y|h∘f] − E[Y|f])²].
- Thm 1 (uniform-mass binning): R_cal ≤ (sqrt(log(4B/δ)/(2(⌊n/B⌋−1))) + 1/⌊n/B⌋)², and
  R_sha ≤ 8K²/B² under smoothness (A3).
- Eq. (10)-(11): **B* ≍ n^{1/3}, giving R = O(n^{−2/3})**. Remark 9 shows B^{−2} is tight.
- vs **Prop G**: Prop G's three terms are E[η(1−η)] (the irreducible part, i.e. Var[Y] minus the
  sharpness of η), Sun's R_sha (= E(η_γ−η)², the "quantisation" term) and Sun's R_cal (= Σ p_j(p̃_j−η_j)²
  when bin estimates are distinct, the "estimation" term). Up to notation, **Prop G is Sun et al.
  Prop. 1 plus Murphy's partition**. The bin-count rate is in Sun et al. Thm 1 and eq. (10) for d=1 and
  Lipschitz-in-F_Z, which matches d=β=1, M* ∝ n^{1/3} in the draft's own NOTE. Prop G's only nuance is
  that it conditions on γ rather than h, which removes Sun's need for distinct bin values. That is not
  a contribution.

**Gupta, C., Ramdas, A. (2021). Distribution-free calibration guarantees for histogram binning without
sample splitting. arXiv 2105.04656 (ICML 2021, PMLR 139; venue not checked against the proceedings
page).** (Read.)
- Thm 3: UMD is (ε,α)-conditionally calibrated with ε = sqrt(log(2B/α)/(2(⌊n/B⌋−1))). Thm 4 bounds
  E[ℓ2-ECE] by sqrt(B/2n). §3.2 gives *heuristic* guidance for choosing B by eyeballing ε vs B (no
  sharpness term and no rate for B).
- vs **Prop G**: supplies the estimation term only. The bin-count trade-off is informal.

**Gupta, C., Podkopaev, A., Ramdas, A. (2020). Distribution-free binary classification: prediction sets,
confidence intervals and calibration. NeurIPS 2020. arXiv 2006.10564.** (Read.) Thm 3 says injective
calibrators cannot be distribution-free calibrated, so binning is necessary. Corollary 3 and Thm 5 give
calibration of a fixed or uniform-mass partition at O(sqrt(B log(B/α)/n)). It motivates binning by a
frozen confidence signal and has no M* rate.

**Kumar, A., Liang, P., Ma, T. (2019). Verified uncertainty calibration. NeurIPS 2019. arXiv
1909.10155.** (Read.) Prop. 3.3 says binning underestimates calibration error. Histogram binning needs
O(B/ε²) samples. Lemma 4.3 covers well-balanced uniform-mass bins. Prop. D.4 bounds the MSE increase
from binning (the quantisation side). Fig. 3b shows the calibration–MSE trade-off in B. There is no
explicit optimal-B rate.

**Futami, F., Fujisawa, M. (2024). Information-theoretic generalization analysis for expected
calibration error. NeurIPS 2024. arXiv 2405.15709.** (Read.) Eq. (7) splits total bias into binning
bias and statistical bias. Statistical bias is O(sqrt(B/n_te)) (Thm 2) and binning bias is O(1/B). The
optimal B is n^{1/3} and the total bias is O(n^{−1/3}). App. D.5: Hölder smoothness does not improve
the binning bias beyond 1/B. App. F.6 relates this to the minimax rate n^{−β/(2β+d)}.
- vs **Prop G**: this is about ECE *estimation* (the metric), not recalibration risk, but it gives the
  same n^{1/3} bin count. Together with Sun et al. it rules out any novelty claim for a bin-count rate.

**Murphy, A. H. (1973). A new vector partition of the probability score. J. Applied Meteorology
12(4):595-600.** (Citation taken from Kumar et al. 2019 ref. [2]; the source was not opened.) This is
the reliability/resolution/uncertainty decomposition of the Brier score.

###### 2.4 Rem rem:drift: verification of the formula
The stationarity condition is −Q'(M) = B/n. With Q = e^{f(u)}, u = log M and a = −f'(u), this gives
aQ/M = B/n, i.e. log a + f(u) − u = log B − log n. Differentiating in log n gives
u'(a'/a − a − 1) = −1, so **du/d log n = 1/(a + 1 − a'/a)** (with a' = da/du), as stated. If a rises
toward 2β/d (a' > 0), the slope exceeds 1/(a+1). The algebra is correct. No precedent was found. It is
elementary, and it explains the steep finite-grid slopes that Conrad et al. (2026) also observe. Keep it
as a remark and cite Conrad et al. as an independent observation of the same phenomenon.

##### 3. Recommended related-work sentences (drop-in)

1. "Coverage within frozen cells is the Mondrian guarantee of Vovk et al. (2005) and Vovk (2012). The
   exact Beta law of calibration-conditional cell coverage appears in Vovk (2012) and Ding et al.
   (2023), and Prop. B0 only aggregates it across cells. Learned taxonomies fitted on a disjoint split
   follow Ding et al. (2023) and Berthier et al. (2026)."
2. "The bias–variance balance behind Theorem B, with cell width h ≍ n^{-1/(2β+d)} and coverage error
   n^{-β/(2β+d)} under Hölder continuity of the conditional score law, is established for kernel-localized
   conformal prediction by Conrad et al. (2026; see also Min et al., 2026; Hore and Barber, 2025) and goes
   back to the partition-based local conformal method of Lei and Wasserman (2014). We give the
   hard-partition analogue with exact finite-n variance and do not claim a new rate."
3. "Prop. G is the Brier/MSE decomposition of Murphy (1973) as used for binned recalibration by Sun et al.
   (2023), who derive B* ≍ n^{1/3} (see also Kumar et al., 2019; Gupta and Ramdas, 2021; Futami and
   Fujisawa, 2024). We restate it to make the forecast side observable."
4. "Calibrating on an outcome-defined subset is a calibration/test law mismatch, whose coverage loss is
   the transfer gap of Wang (2026). It differs from selection on test features, which is valid by
   Bao et al. (2024) and Jin and Ren (2025). For LLMs, Cherian et al. (2024) give coverage conditional
   on bins of a data-adaptive confidence level, while Mohri and Hashimoto (2024) and Abbasi-Yadkori et
   al. (2024) give marginal guarantees using self-evaluation scores."

Framing advice: present M-fail as an **Example**, not a Proposition. Present B0 as a **Corollary** of the
known Beta law, with a pointer to Berthier et al.'s audit warning. State Thm B as "partition analogue of
known localized rates". State Prop G as "restated from Sun et al. (2023)". The new content is (i) the
stage-measurability *framing* for LLM decisions (pre- and post-answer), (ii) the B0 → pointwise-estimand
argument, (iii) rem:drift, and (iv) the empirics.

### `reports/transport_prior_work.md`

#### Prior work vs. the novelty claim "carries a calibration across elicitation procedures by transport"

Draft claim (`paper/main.tex`, Related work, "Shift, selection and transport", l. 859–860):
"We are not aware of prior work that carries a calibration across elicitation procedures by transport."

Draft method: a calibration (Platt + conformal thresholds) fitted under procedure A is carried, without labels, to
procedure B by a 1-D monotone map of B's reports onto A's scale: (i) the unpaired quantile map F_A^{-1}∘F_B
(monotone OT between marginals), or (ii) isotonic regression of V_A on V_B from unlabelled questions elicited
under both procedures. A label-free bound gives |coverage change| ≤ P(set changes), the "crossing mass".

Checked on 2026-10-02 with alphaXiv full text and arXiv, ICML, PMLR and mlanthology pages.

**Verdict.** No paper found carries a calibration across *LLM elicitation procedures* by a monotone *score*
transport map, and none bounds the coverage change by the crossing mass. But the claim as written is too broad
to hold. Two kinds of work are close:
(a) Doula (ICML 2026) uses unlabelled *paired* data to carry conformal calibration across representations
by transport. This is close to our paired variant (ii).
(b) Yilmaz & Heckel (2022, QTC) uses *quantile matching* of source and target confidence marginals to carry a
conformal threshold to a new distribution without labels. This is mechanically close to our unpaired variant (i).
Correia & Louizos (NeurIPS 2025) bound conformal coverage gaps by 1-D OT distances between score distributions,
using unlabelled test data. All three must be cited, and the sentence must be narrowed.

---

##### 1. Doula, "Conformal Calibration Transfer" — VERIFIED — closeness: CLOSE (to variant ii); partial overall

- **Citation.** Achref Doula (TU Darmstadt / Tongji). *Conformal Calibration Transfer.* arXiv:2609.10737 (submitted
  9 Sep 2026; cs.LG, stat.ML). arXiv comments say "Accepted at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning
  (ICML 2026)"; an ICML 2026 poster page confirms this (https://icml.cc/virtual/2026/poster/61667).
  URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.10737
- **What it does.** Labelled conformal calibration exists only in a source input space X_s. Prediction sets are
  needed in a target space X_t (a sensor or modality change). The two spaces are linked by an *unlabelled paired*
  corpus {(x_s, x_t)} of the same instances. "Transported Conformal Calibration" learns a map f: X_s→X_t from the
  pairs (an image-to-image network with ℓ1 loss and optional KL alignment of predictions). It pushes the labelled
  calibration inputs through f and recalibrates on the target model's scores. It then corrects any remaining
  mismatch without labels. TCC-KS uses a one-sided DKW bound on the CDF gap of a label-free uncertainty
  surrogate (1 − max softmax) to lower α. Weighted-TCC applies post-transport density-ratio weights. It also
  proves an impossibility theorem: label-free transfer needs a structural assumption.
- **Precise difference from the draft.**
  - Doula transports *inputs* (high-dimensional, learned map), not the 1-D *scores* through a monotone map.
  - The predictor and score function are fixed. In the draft, the "report function" (elicitation procedure)
    changes while the covariates stay the same.
  - It does not handle Platt recalibration, and has no unpaired quantile-map variant.
  - Its label-free bound uses the KS/DKW discrepancy of a surrogate plus a slack assumption (A2). It is not the
    crossing mass P(set changes).
  - Conceptually it is the same template as our paired variant: unlabelled paired observations of the same
    instance under two "views", a transport carrying labelled calibration across, and a label-free diagnostic.
    This is the strongest threat to the sentence as written.

```bibtex
@inproceedings{doula2026conformal,
  title     = {Conformal Calibration Transfer},
  author    = {Doula, Achref},
  booktitle = {Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML)},
  year      = {2026},
  eprint    = {2609.10737},
  archivePrefix = {arXiv},
  primaryClass  = {cs.LG},
  url       = {https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.10737}
}
```
(The PMLR volume and pages were not yet available on 2026-10-02. Add them when the proceedings appear.)

##### 2. Batch Calibration (Zhou et al., ICLR 2024) — VERIFIED — closeness: PARTIAL (weak)

- **Citation.** Han Zhou, Xingchen Wan, Lev Proleev, Diana Mincu, Jilin Chen, Katherine Heller, Subhrajit Roy.
  *Batch Calibration: Rethinking Calibration for In-Context Learning and Prompt Engineering.* ICLR 2024.
  arXiv:2309.17249. URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.17249 ; https://mlanthology.org/iclr/2024/zhou2024iclr-batch/
- **What it does.** It treats prompt brittleness (formatting, verbaliser choice, ICL examples) as a *contextual
  bias* in the label-space scores. It estimates that bias label-free, as the mean class probability over a batch
  of unlabelled test inputs. It then removes the bias (log-space subtraction, i.e. a re-centring of the class
  prior). This unifies contextual and domain-context calibration. BCL is a variant that uses a few labels.
- **Precise difference.** BC is *within-prompt* debiasing that aims at accuracy and robustness. It does not carry
  a calibration fitted under one prompt to another, and it does not map one prompt's reports onto another's
  scale. It gives no probability-calibration or coverage guarantee and uses no paired or quantile transport. The
  only overlap is that it is label-free, uses unlabelled inputs and targets prompt variation. Cite it as
  label-free prompt-robust recalibration.

```bibtex
@inproceedings{zhou2024batch,
  title     = {Batch Calibration: Rethinking Calibration for In-Context Learning and Prompt Engineering},
  author    = {Zhou, Han and Wan, Xingchen and Proleev, Lev and Mincu, Diana and Chen, Jilin and Heller, Katherine A. and Roy, Subhrajit},
  booktitle = {International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR)},
  year      = {2024},
  eprint    = {2309.17249},
  archivePrefix = {arXiv},
  url       = {https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.17249}
}
```

##### 3. Thermometer (Shen et al., ICML 2024) — VERIFIED — closeness: PARTIAL (weak)

- **Citation.** Maohao Shen, Subhro Das, Kristjan Greenewald, Prasanna Sattigeri, Gregory W. Wornell, Soumya Ghosh.
  *Thermometer: Towards Universal Calibration for Large Language Models.* ICML 2024, PMLR 235:44687–44711.
  arXiv:2403.08819. URL: https://proceedings.mlr.press/v235/shen24c.html
- **What it does.** It trains an auxiliary network on *labelled* data from many tasks. The network maps the LLM's
  features on a task's unlabelled inputs to a temperature. At test time it predicts a temperature for a *new task*
  from unlabelled inputs only, and so preserves accuracy.
- **Precise difference.** It transfers *across tasks* (input distributions), not across elicitation procedures
  for the same questions. The object transferred is a learned temperature predictor, not a calibration carried by
  a monotone score map. It needs multi-task labelled training. There are no conformal thresholds and no coverage
  bound. Cite it as label-free calibration of LLMs on new tasks.

```bibtex

  title     = {Thermometer: Towards Universal Calibration for Large Language Models},
  author    = {Shen, Maohao and Das, Subhro and Greenewald, Kristjan and Sattigeri, Prasanna and Wornell, Gregory W. and Ghosh, Soumya},
  booktitle = {Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning},

  volume    = {235},
  pages     = {44687--44711},
```

##### 4. Quantile mapping / label-free recalibration under shift

###### 4a. Yilmaz & Heckel, QTC (2022) — VERIFIED — closeness: CLOSE (to variant i, mechanism)
- **Citation.** Fatih Furkan Yilmaz, Reinhard Heckel. *Test-time Recalibration of Conformal Predictors Under
  Distribution Shift Based on Unlabeled Examples.* arXiv:2210.04166 (v1 Oct 2022, v2 Jun 2023). It was submitted
  to ICLR 2023 (OpenReview id KrGgylZ0tw_). I could not verify an archival venue, so cite it as a preprint.
  URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.04166
- **What it does.** "Quantile Thresholded Confidence" predicts the target conformal threshold from unlabelled
  target data by matching quantiles of the max-softmax confidence between source and target marginals.
  - QTC-T computes q = F_Q^{-1}(α) on the target, then β = F_P(q) on the source. It recalibrates on the labelled
    source set at level β.
  - QTC-S is the mirror image.
  - It is provably consistent under a spurious-feature shift model.
- **Precise difference.** This is unpaired marginal quantile matching used to carry a conformal calibration
  across a shift without labels. That is our variant (i) applied at the threshold level, so the mechanism is
  closest here.
  - The shift is a covariate/sub-population shift with a fixed predictor, not a change of elicitation procedure
    on the same questions.
  - It matches a proxy score (max softmax) and only at one quantile level. It does not map the full report scale
    or carry a Platt map.
  - There is no paired/isotonic variant and no crossing-mass bound.

```bibtex
@misc{yilmaz2022testtime,
  title         = {Test-time Recalibration of Conformal Predictors Under Distribution Shift Based on Unlabeled Examples},
  author        = {Yilmaz, Fatih Furkan and Heckel, Reinhard},
  year          = {2022},
  eprint        = {2210.04166},
  archivePrefix = {arXiv},
  primaryClass  = {cs.LG},
  url           = {https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.04166}
}
```

###### 4b. Correia & Louizos (NeurIPS 2025) — VERIFIED — closeness: PARTIAL (bound side)
- **Citation.** Alvaro H. C. Correia, Christos Louizos. *Non-exchangeable Conformal Prediction with Optimal
  Transport: Tackling Distribution Shifts with Unlabeled Data.* NeurIPS 2025 (38th). arXiv:2507.10425.
  URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.10425
- **What it does.** It bounds the "total coverage gap" (averaged over α) by 1-D Wasserstein / weighted-CDF
  distances between calibration and test score distributions. For a label-free version, it brackets the unknown
  test score law by stochastically dominating auxiliaries built from all-label scores (min/max, or uniform vs
  model-sampled label). It then *reweights calibration points* to minimise the bound.
- **Precise difference.** It uses 1-D OT on scores, unlabelled test data and a label-free coverage bound. But it
  reweights the calibration data and does not transport scores. The bound is an OT distance averaged over α,
  not a fixed-α crossing mass. The setting is input shift, not procedure change.

```bibtex
@inproceedings{correia2025nonexchangeable,
  title     = {Non-exchangeable Conformal Prediction with Optimal Transport: Tackling Distribution Shifts with Unlabeled Data},
  author    = {Correia, Alvaro H. C. and Louizos, Christos},
  booktitle = {Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems},
  volume    = {38},
  year      = {2025},
  eprint    = {2507.10425},
  archivePrefix = {arXiv},
  url       = {https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.10425}
}
```

###### 4c. Zhao et al., "Calibrate Before Use" (ICML 2021) — VERIFIED — closeness: PARTIAL (weak). Already in refs.bib as `zhao2021calibrate`.
- Tony Z. Zhao, Eric Wallace, Shi Feng, Dan Klein, Sameer Singh. ICML 2021, PMLR 139:12697–12706. arXiv:2102.09690.
- Contextual calibration estimates the label bias of a prompt from content-free inputs ("N/A") and applies an
  affine correction so those inputs score uniformly. It is label-free and within-prompt, aims at accuracy and
  variance across prompts, and transfers nothing between prompts. It has the same relation to the draft as
  Batch Calibration. No new BibTeX is needed; check that the existing entry matches.

###### 4d. Ziegler & Czyż, "Unsupervised Recalibration" (2019) — VERIFIED — closeness: NONE
- Albert Ziegler, Paweł Czyż. arXiv:1908.09157 (preprint). It corrects for label-prior shift using a
  confusion-on-partition matrix plus the observed field histogram of predictions, then applies a Saerens-style
  prior correction. It is a quantification method under the class-conditional-invariance assumption. It has no
  score transport and no conformal component. Optional cite. No BibTeX recommended.

###### 4e. Other items found (for context; not recommended as must-cite)
- **Afrin & Shihab, "When Accuracy Gaps Fail to Certify: Auditing Cross-Domain Recalibration of LLM Judges",
  arXiv:2609.27954 (Aug 2026).** It studies whether a Platt/temperature map fitted for an LLM judge on one domain
  transfers to another. It proves that no assumption-free label-free repair exists (Prop. 5) and concludes that
  transfer "requires target evidence or a defended transport assumption". The topic is related (transferring a
  scalar LLM recalibration map), but there is no transport method. Its Prop. 5 is a useful foil for stating our
  invariance assumption. Optional cite (verified on arXiv; venue unknown).
- **SupportCal (Luo et al., arXiv:2609.24303, Sep 2026) and DACA (Luo et al. 2025, not separately verified).** These
  calibrate a post-trained LLM label-free by fitting a temperature through KL alignment to its pretrained base
  model. They are label-free cross-model calibration, not transport across elicitation procedures. Optional.
- **Moslemi & Milani, arXiv:2411.01685.** It aligns group score distributions to a Wasserstein barycentre through
  quantile OT maps, label-free, for fairness in record matching. It is a precedent for quantile-map score
  alignment, but the purpose is unrelated. Not needed.
- **Park et al., "Calibrated Prediction with Covariate Shift via Unsupervised Domain Adaptation" (AISTATS 2020,
  arXiv:2003.00343).** This is importance-weighted calibration under covariate shift. It is already covered in
  spirit by the draft's `tibshirani2019conformal` sentence. Optional.
- **Searches with no closer hit.** I found no paper that (a) carries a Platt or conformal calibration from one LLM
  confidence-elicitation prompt to another without labels, (b) uses isotonic regression on doubly elicited
  unlabelled questions, or (c) bounds coverage change by P(set changes).
  - "Same Answer, Different Confidence" (Kim & Kang, arXiv:2605.27752) only documents protocol sensitivity.

---

##### Recommended rewrite of the novelty sentence

Replace l. 859–860 with:

> Unlabelled data have been used to carry a conformal calibration to a new input distribution, by matching
> confidence quantiles \citep{yilmaz2022testtime}, by bounding and reweighting through optimal transport of
> scores \citep{correia2025nonexchangeable}, or across sensor modalities by transporting paired inputs
> \citep{doula2026conformal}; label-free prompt recalibration \citep{zhao2021calibrate,zhou2024batch,shen2024thermometer}
> instead debiases or rescales within a prompt or task. What is new here is the case where the questions are fixed
> and only the elicitation procedure changes: the calibration is carried by a monotone map of the confidence report
> itself, and the coverage change is bounded by a label-free crossing mass.

(If space is tight, shorten to: "Closest are label-free conformal recalibration under input shift by quantile
matching \citep{yilmaz2022testtime} or OT \citep{correia2025nonexchangeable} and transport of paired inputs
across modalities \citep{doula2026conformal}; we instead transport the confidence report across elicitation
procedures on fixed questions and bound the coverage change by a label-free crossing mass.")

### `reports/related_work_bib_report.md`

#### Related-work BibTeX verification report (2026-10-02)

Output: `reports/related_work_bib.bib` (36 new entries + 5 corrections = 41 entries, no duplicate keys, braces balanced).
Sources: publisher/proceedings pages (PMLR, NeurIPS, JMLR, LIPIcs), Crossref DOI records, OpenReview API, arXiv API (all arXiv ids confirmed to match title and authors).

All 41 verified. Nothing was dropped. Differences from the requested descriptions:

- **zhao2021calibrate**: the PMLR proceedings list the first author as "Zihao Zhao". arXiv lists "Tony Z. Zhao", the same person. The entry follows PMLR.
- **sclar2024quantifying**: the full official title ends "... or: How I Learned to Start Worrying about Prompt Formatting". The entry uses the full title.
- **peyre2019computational**: the FnTML journal title is "Computational Optimal Transport: With Applications to Data Science", vol. 11(5–6):355–607. arXiv uses the short title.
- **santambrogio2015optimal**: subtitle "Calculus of Variations, PDEs, and Modeling". This is PNLDE vol. 87.
- **tibshirani2019conformal**: the NeurIPS proceedings give no page numbers, so the entry has none.
- **platt1999probabilistic**: there is no DOI. The pages (61–74), MIT Press and 1999 were confirmed from catalogue records. The book editors were not added.
- **lin2022teaching**: TMLR has no volume or pages. The year 2022 was confirmed via OpenReview (8s8K2UZGTZ) and mlanthology.

| detommaso2024multicalibration | Verified: proceedings.mlr.press/v235/detommaso24a | Applies multicalibration to LLM confidence scores. Groups prompt/completion pairs by embedding clustering and by "self-annotation" (querying the LLM), and calibrates simultaneously across the intersecting groups. |
| kiyani2024conformal | Verified: proceedings.mlr.press/v235/kiyani24a | Partition Learning Conformal Prediction (PLCP) learns a partition of feature space to improve conditional validity of prediction sets, instead of fixing the groups in advance. |

| hebertjohnson2018multicalibration | Verified: proceedings.mlr.press/v80/hebert-johnson18a | Introduces multicalibration, which requires calibration on every subpopulation in a computationally identifiable class, and gives an algorithm to post-process predictors to achieve it. |
